hints: Think about what a vaccine actually trains your immune system to recognise, the antigens on the pathogen surface.
Ask yourself what would happen if those antigens kept changing, would the memory cells from the old vaccine still recognise the new pathogen?
walkthrough:
**Recall how vaccination works**

Great start. A vaccine gives you harmless antigens so you make memory B and T cells. Those memory cells only protect you later if the real pathogen still has the same antigens.

**Compare smallpox and TB**

Smallpox virus was very stable worldwide, with little change in its antigens. That means one vaccine could recognise almost every case, everywhere. The TB bacterium is much more variable and harder for one vaccine to cover fully.

**Link stability to eradication**

Because the smallpox antigens did not vary, the vaccine stayed effective and herd immunity could build up until transmission stopped. That stable target is a key reason eradication was possible.

options.A: Not true. Vaccination can stimulate immunity to both, for example BCG for TB, it is just less consistently effective than the smallpox vaccine.
options.B: Not true. Crowded, poor living conditions favour spread of many diseases including both TB and smallpox, so this does not explain the difference.
options.C: Correct. Little antigenic variation meant the same vaccine produced effective memory that recognised the virus everywhere, allowing eradication.
options.D: True fact but not an explanation. We have effective vaccines against both viruses and bacteria, so pathogen type alone does not decide success.
